lessons.title: Branches, merging, and conflicts
lessons.concept: A branch is a movable name pointing to a commit; HEAD identifies the active branch. Commits advance that pointer, and merge combines two histories while preserving common ancestry. Always separate the intention, the incoming data, the transformation being performed, and the observable result. This separation lets you predict behavior before running code and diagnose an error precisely.

explanation.title: Mental model
explanation.text: A branch is a movable name pointing to a commit; HEAD identifies the active branch. Commits advance that pointer, and merge combines two histories while preserving common ancestry. Always separate the intention, the incoming data, the transformation being performed, and the observable result. This separation lets you predict behavior before running code and diagnose an error precisely.

explanation.title: Simple analogy
explanation.text: Two drafts start from the same photocopy; merging combines additions, while a conflict needs a choice when both rewrite the same sentence.

explanation.title: Understand it deeply
explanation.text: git switch -c creates a pointer at the current commit and checks it out. Always verify the branch name before starting so commits do not land on main. Read the example from top to bottom, identify every input, and predict the output before running the command. This habit turns memorized syntax into reusable understanding.

explanation.title: Understand it deeply
explanation.text: A fast-forward merge only moves a pointer; --no-ff creates a visible merge commit. Policy decides which to use, but final content must be tested after combination. In a real project, verify this mechanism with the browser, terminal, or DevTools instead of assuming it works. Observable evidence is more reliable than intuition.

explanation.title: Understand it deeply
explanation.text: A conflict marks ours and theirs variants in the file. Read business context, produce one valid final version, remove all markers, stage, and finish the merge. Finally apply the concept through one small isolated change, check the result, and revert if needed. Short changes make cause and effect easy to connect.

explanation.title: Simple analogy
explanation.text: A “do not archive” list does not remove an already filed page; if a secret was archived, revoke it and clean history through a coordinated procedure.

explanation.title: Understand it deeply
explanation.text: Ignore installed dependencies, build outputs, and local variables, but keep source and lockfile. git check-ignore -v explains which rule excludes a path. Read the example from top to bottom, identify every input, and predict the output before running the command. This habit turns memorized syntax into reusable understanding.

explanation.title: Understand it deeply
explanation.text: A NEXT_PUBLIC_ value is sent to the browser and must never be secret. Server keys remain in deployment environment variables and are neither committed nor logged. In a real project, verify this mechanism with the browser, terminal, or DevTools instead of assuming it works. Observable evidence is more reliable than intuition.

explanation.title: Understand it deeply
explanation.text: Before recovery, inspect status, diff, and log. git restore concerns uncommitted work, while git revert creates a traceable inverse for an already shared commit. Finally apply the concept through one small isolated change, check the result, and revert if needed. Short changes make cause and effect easy to connect.

codeExample.title: Annotated example
codeExample.code:
# Secret incident response

1. Revoke or rotate the exposed credential in its provider dashboard.
2. Record the exposure window without copying the secret into this file.
3. Run git status --short, git diff, and git log --oneline -5.
4. Add the local secret path to .gitignore and verify it with git check-ignore -v .env.local.
5. If a shared commit must be undone, identify it with git show --stat HEAD and use git revert after review.
6. Run npm run build, request review, and document the replacement credential owner.
